en: One scroll of the illustrated narrative of Mahāmaudgalyāyana’s salvation of his mother from the underworld, including [the account of] the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven on the fifteenth day of the seventh month:
"The gates of heaven open and the doors of hell are flung wide. Three.

As the offerings are presented and the merit is dedicated, the eight classes of deities and the dragon gods from the heavens all descend to receive the teachings. They manifest in this world to provide blessings and support for the deceased, so that they may be reborn in supreme joy. Thus, with the hundred flavors of the *bowl-offering* (*ulambana*), we look up to the Three Honored Ones and the great assembly; mindful of our ancestors, we first seek to rescue those in their dire and suspended distress.
Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world, before the Venerable Maudgalyāyana had left the household life,
his name was Rāva.
He possessed deep faith in the Triple Gem and held the Mahāyāna in high esteem.
□□□ wished to travel to another country for trade.
He then divided his wealth and treasures,
instructing his mother to remain behind to prepare offerings of vegetarian feasts for the Buddha and the Sangha, and to invite those who came to partake.
After Rāvaṇa had departed,
his mother gave rise to a mind of stinginess;
she privately concealed all the wealth and assets that had been entrusted to him.
Before ten days had passed, the son completed his affairs and returned home.
His mother said to her son,
"I have performed meritorious acts by observing the fasts according to your instructions."
Because of this, he deceived both ordinary people and sages;
at the end of his life, he consequently fell into the Avīci Hell to undergo immeasurable suffering.
After the three circumambulations of the *Rāvaṇa* were completed.
He immediately went forth as a monk under the Buddha.
Due to the causes of his past cultivation, upon hearing the Dharma, he realized the fruit of Arhatship.
Thereupon, with his eye of the Path, he sought after his compassionate parents but could not find them.
Throughout the cycle of birth and death in the six realms, she has not seen her mother.
Maudgalyāyana, overcome with grief, addressed the World-Honored One:
"World-Honored One, where is my compassionate mother now enjoying happiness?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Maudgalyāyana:
"Your mother has already fallen into the Avīci Hell and is currently undergoing various sufferings."
Although you have attained the fruit of sainthood,
what do you intend to do with this?
Unless it is the day when the assembly of monks from the ten directions unties and removes it, [it shall remain].
Only through the combined power of the multitude can one rescue them;
therefore, out of compassion, the Buddha established this expedient means.
That which is called the *Ullambana* is precisely this matter.
Since his parents passed away, Rāhula has observed the three-year mourning period; now that the rites are complete, he finds no joy in music and his appearance is emaciated.
Even when eating delicacies, he finds them tasteless, for his very frame is worn by grief.
Yet upon hearing that the Tathāgata is at the Deer Park, all beings—both humans and devas—are filled with compassion for him.
Now I study the Way seeking the Tathāgata; I have gone to the Twin Trees to question the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha himself hesitated for a moment; He bowed his head to the Preceptor, the Honored One with Two Feet.
To his left and right were Brahmā and Śakra, And the Great Generals of the East and West, the Scent-Emitting Spirits.
Behold the ten thousand characters of lapis lazuli hue; behind the neck, the circular halo resembles the lunar disc.
If you wish to know what lies upon the myriad jewels and thousand flowers, it is just like five-colored clouds at the edge of the heavens.
We disciples, ordinary and ignorant, dwell within the five [aggregates], unable to abandon or depart from greed and anger.
It is simply because my karmic offenses throughout my life have been heavy, That this calamity has reached my compassionate mother, casting her into [the hells].
I fear only that the aspect of impermanence will press upon me, Causing me to sink into the bitter sea at the ford of birth and death.
May the Buddha, out of his compassion, deliver this disciple; I shall study the Way with single-minded devotion to repay my two parents.
World-Honored One, when you hear the words spoken by Rāhu, know that his mind is upright and not crooked;
first examine his speech with your fingers, then listen to him, for he shall surely be free from the seven obstructions.
Even if one were to pile up treasures reaching the Milky Way, it would not equal the merit of a person who briefly leaves the household life.
It is like a blind turtle encountering a floating log, Or like a lotus blooming from within vast waters.
Perishing in the fire-housed dwelling, one finds it difficult to escape; The surging sea of suffering is broad and boundless.
Precisely because sentient beings engage in conceptual discrimination, The Tathāgata has established the three vehicles.
The Buddha called for Ānanda to shave his hair; His robes were instantly transformed into *kāṣāya*.
At that moment he realized the fruit of Arhatship, And later received the *Prātimokṣa* precepts.
At that time, Rāhula stood before the Buddha; From the golden incense burner, fragrant smoke rose billowing upward.
Six kinds of jade groves shake heaven and earth; The four flowers mark their forms as the leaves purify the sky.
A thousand varieties of brocade patch the seat; Ten thousand paths of wondrous banners are profound within the void.
The Buddha himself declared, "My younger brother," Named the Great Maudgalyāyana of Supernatural Powers.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana realized the fruit of arhatship beneath the twin śāla trees.
Why was this so? According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it says:
This refers to the "Chapter on the Poor Son," where one first receives the wage and only then clears away the filth.
This is precisely that.
Having first attained the fruit of Arhatship, one shall subsequently train in the Path.
Behold the place where Maudgalyāyana sat in meditation deep within the mountains.
Having shaved off his hair and beard, Maudgalyāyana immediately entered the deep mountains with his body.
In a secluded, deep, and pure place where no one dwells, One should immediately contemplate emptiness and sit in meditation.
Through sitting in meditation and contemplating emptiness, one knows good and evil; Subduing the mind and settling the mind, one remains unattached.
Facing a mirror, clear and still, unmoving and remote, The right foot must then press upon the right foot.
Sitting upright upon a flat rock, he placed his tongue against the upper palate;
his white bones were entirely empty and his breaths ceased to mingle.
At that time, the herds of deer stopped their chanting in the forest, drawing near to the clear pond to gaze toward the headlands of the sea.
Listening to the Dharma beneath the bright moon in the courtyard, Sitting in meditation alone beneath the pines on the green mountains;
The sea mist at the edge of heaven never changes its distance, And from the watchtower beyond the ridges, one gazes upon the green peaks.
The autumn wind whistles through the forest, As yellow leaves fall and drift away upon the water.
Maudgalyāyana sits in meditative repose within the realm of the void; Having internally realized the mind, he gradually cultivates and attains mastery.
As a śrāvaka dwelling on the stage of expectation, He moves freely through the mountain ranges.
Emerging from samādhi, Maudgalyāyana Swiftly manifests supernormal powers.
Coming like a sudden clap of thunder, departing like a whirlwind;
Sea geese cry out piercingly through the silk-like mist, Ospreys break free from their nets and cages.
Within the discourse, mists and clouds are azure; The heavens are clear, and the distant paths are crimson.
Having attained mastery over supernormal powers, he tossed his bowl and ascended into the air.
At that time, Śreṇika went upward as far as the Brahma-heaven, while Maudgalyāyana reached the celestial palace;
in his ears, he heard only the sound of drums and music.
The vermilion pavilion half-reflects the golden palace; From the azure windows, the imperial achievements are fully recounted.
Three or five knocks upon the door with the mendicant’s staff— Unawares, tears well up from his chest.
The Elder comes forth as if to converse; With palms joined, he first speaks of filial devotion within.
The Child asked, "Do you know the Elder?
The Mother replied, "In Jambudvīpa, there are those who, while still young, have suffered the loss of both parents;
their families are immensely wealthy, yet the children and grandchildren are orphaned and destitute, with no way forward. I am their compassionate mother, named Qingti."
My father was named the Prime Minister; throughout his life, he cultivated many causes for merit.
Having passed away, he has been reborn in this heavenly realm. His noble lineage, vast wealth, and distinguished status bring joy and satisfaction to all who behold him.
The resonance of bells and drums reveals the refined sounds of music.
The zither is struck, its sound echoing through the distant pavilion; Alas, alas, the toil and hardship!
Long shall the grace of nursing not be forsaken, for the debt of gratitude is difficult to forget. Since our parting, have you been well and at ease?
I have come here recently to seek you out. Upon hearing these words, the elder’s heart was filled with sorrow.
With a heart full of trepidation, his words come forth slowly; Disciple, in this Jambudvīpa, there is but one breath that is not conscious.
Since there are those who have left the household life, Master, do not take offense at my difficult questioning.
The human relations of this world are of several kinds; At first glance, his speech may seem strange.

The moment of gathering the vital breath is somewhat difficult; In the mundane world, there are many with identical names and surnames, and those with similar features and countenances are of a hundred kinds.
One’s appearance is but a coarse weave of silk;
one can only ponder until there is nowhere left to rest the mind. O Ācārya, you have come to identify me through great hardship.
He spoke further regarding the matters of his household and his intentions. Maudgalyāyana looked at him and said,
"Householder,
when you were young, your name was Rāva."
After his parents had passed away, he went forth as a monk under the Buddha;
having shaved off his hair and beard, he was named Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
who was foremost in supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
When the elder saw that his childhood name was mentioned,
he immediately knew whether his son had been well during their long separation.
Rāhula Maudgalyāyana recognized his compassionate father.
Having completed my inquiries regarding your health and well-being, I ask:
where is my compassionate mother now,
and does she enjoy happiness?
The elder replied, "Rāvaṇa,
while your mother was still alive,"
Our karmic practices differ from yours.
I have cultivated the ten wholesome paths and the five precepts;
after death, my consciousness has attained rebirth in the heavens.
"In her lifetime, your mother habitually committed many grave offenses.
After her life ended, she fell into hell.
You have now entered the dark path toward Jambudvīpa."
Upon questioning his mother, he learned the place of her departure.
Having heard these words, Maudgalyāyana took leave of the elder and descended instantly to Jambudvīpa in the south.
Seeking his mother along the path toward the underworld, he could not find her.
At dawn, he saw eight or nine men and women idling about with nothing to do.
Maudgalyāyana stepped forward and questioned them.
As for the reason for this matter, simply do not prostrate;
who is this worthy one? Here we have gathered in assembly, tranquil and without a single concern, yet he has come from outside the city walls.
The Master of the Channel has arrived here this morning; I am deeply perplexed by the hand within my own heart.
The people replied, "We address you, O Monk: It is simply because we share the same name and the same nature;
Our names being intermingled, we were summoned here. It has been exactly three or five days since our identities were verified."
Without cause, I am released and sent back; Already, my wife and children have delivered me to the grave.
Alone, I am carved out in the desolate wilderness; On all four sides, there are no kinsmen or companions.
Foxes, wolves, crows, and magpies compete to divide and scatter [my remains]; The dwelling is ruined, with nowhere left to turn.
The king’s side was petitioned with a voice of sorrow;
he ruled that she be released as a ghost to dwell in leisure without affairs, receiving her remaining retribution—what more could be done? The paths of life and death are now severed;
once the gate of the spring is closed, it shall not open again. Though there may be a thousand kinds of food upon the tomb, [it is of no avail].
How could it ever satisfy the hunger within one’s belly? Wailing and weeping loudly is ultimately of no benefit;
it merely troubles the paper used to make money. Send word to the men and women at home, urging them to cultivate merit for the sake of the deceased.
Maudgalyāyana remained silent for a long while before speaking: "I understand."
"Is Lady Qingti still there?
The people replied,
"None of us know her."
Maudgalyāyana asked again,
"Where does King Yama reside?
To which the people immediately replied:
The Master walked several more paces northward and saw from afar a three-storied gate tower,
where tens of millions of mighty warriors all held blades and clubs.
"This is the gate of King Yama.
Upon hearing these words, Maudgalyāyana walked several more paces toward the north and immediately saw a three-tiered gate tower.
A strong man drove countless sinners inside;
Maudgalyāyana went forward to inquire,
but his mother was not to be seen.
Weeping loudly by the roadside, they proceeded forward.
The attendants led them to see the king;
the gatekeepers ushered them in, and they were brought before the Great King at the place where he was inquiring about the matter concerning Maudgalyāyana.
When the Great King saw Maudgalyāyana enter, he joined his palms and stood hesitantly;
as he was about to designate a preceptor, the matter suddenly vanished. In haste, he looked behind the screen, and for a moment felt ashamed.
When the *ācārya* arrived at this place, the disciple remained within the realm of darkness.
The judgment of life and death is pronounced for the person under trial;
Though they may not know the monk, he has long since known their name.
Is it because the Buddha’s messenger has arrived here with a private matter of his own? The verdict of Mount Tai is difficult to alter.
The heavenly registers and earthly brushes are always at hand; The karmic retribution of sinners arises according to their conditions.
Who among men can save them? Flesh and blood, congealed fat—stinking filth that stains the *ācārya*’s pure robes.
One must not dwell long in the dark paths of the netherworld.
I humbly pray that the Ācārya may depart soon. Maudgalyāyana replied, "The Great King must not speak thus;

does Your Majesty not understand? He said that throughout his life he had parents whom he served by constantly observing the fast and always shortening his midday meal. Judging by his conduct, he remains among the living."
The deceased shall sit together with us in the Pure Land;
In heaven there is only Father alone, while the Compassionate Mother and all the devas cannot be found. Even by calculation, it should not be that we pass through hell;
I only fear that the Yellow Heaven will perversely execute me, And that my release from this pursuit depends on the limits of heaven and earth.
Sighing with grief, lamentation, and regret, he let out a long breath and said, "Great King, when the retribution of karma comes, will it cross this realm?
Will even King Yama know of it? Once Maudgalyāyana had finished speaking, the Great King summoned him to ascend the palace hall.
Upon seeing the Bodhisattva of the Hell Realm, he immediately prostrated himself.
"Come, seek out your mother," Maudgalyāyana replied.
Maudgalyāyana then addressed him, saying:
"I have come to seek my mother.
While your mother was still alive,
she committed vast and boundless evils without limit."
"You shall fall into hell.
You go on ahead; I shall follow immediately.
The Great King then summoned the official of karma.
The Lord of Death’s record-keepers arrived immediately at the appointed time.
How much time has passed since the passing of my preceptor and my mother, Lady Qingti?
At that time, the official in charge of affairs addressed the King, saying, "Great King,
Lady Qingti has already been gone for three years."
The adjudication of offenses generally rests with the Heavenly Court.
The Director of Records, the Grand Commandant of Mount Tai, sent his two attendants, Wang and Huan, the Good and Evil Boys,
to Mount Tai to investigate which hell Lady Qingti was currently in.
The Great King spoke, saying:
"Preceptor, you should accompany the youth to inquire of the General of the Five Paths regarding the destination they should take."
Upon hearing these words, Maudgalyāyana took his leave of the Great King.
He immediately set out and, after walking only a few paces, arrived at the banks of the Nai River.
There he saw countless sinners who had stripped off their clothes and hung them upon the trees.
He wept aloud several times, wishing to pass beyond but unable to do so;
turning back again and again in terror, five by five and three by three,
he beat his head and wailed.
Maudgalyāyana asked about the circumstances of this matter:
The waters of the Ājīvakī River flow westward with great haste; Shattered stones and treacherous cliffs make the path difficult to tread.
Their garments have slipped and hung upon the branches of trees by the side; Driven along, they cannot stop as they stand there at the appointed time.
Beside the riverbank, he asked his name; Before the calamity, he did not realize his clothes were damp.
Only today does he know that death has come; Pair by pair, they weep with deep sorrow beside the tree.
In life, I cherished him as my own treasure; Now, a team of four noble horses draws a carriage adorned with pearls.
It is said that through ten thousand ages not a thousand changes occur; who would have known that so early it was transformed into mere dust?
Alas! How painful is the heart’s grief! In vain one arranges white bones to form a lofty tomb.
At the southern trough, the dragon’s descendants ride; at the northern window, the fragrant carriage meets the rain of the wife.
With one voice they all say it cannot be discussed; sighing deeply and heaving long breaths, what further resentment can there be?
Those who have committed sins fall into the hells, while those who perform good deeds will surely reach the human or celestial realms.
Now, each follows their own karma according to conditions; it is certain that we shall meet again, though such a reunion is difficult to achieve.
Shaking hands with courtesy requires diligent effort; turning one's head to wipe away tears, they gaze at each other fully.
Within their ears, they hear only the urgent chanting of the Way, as tens of thousands of multitudes are driven forward.
On the southern bank of the Yellow River, Ox-Head brandishes his staff; on the northern shore of the water, the hell-wardens hold up their pitchforks.
The person in the water gazes with longing eyes; The one on the bank sheds tears in a steady stream.
Had they known beforehand this place of such hardship, They would regret not having cultivated fields of merit in their youth.
Maudgalyāyana asked: "Beneath the tree by the Vaitaraṇī River."
On this Human Day, it is not false that there are heavens and hells.
If one commits evil, regardless of whether the crime was committed by heaven, the spirits of the netherworld will likewise execute the punishment at the appointed time.
This humble monk’s compassionate parents did not accumulate merit; their departed souls have likewise fallen into the three miserable realms.
I have heard that you are soon to enter hell; I only wish to know daily whether your path has ceased or not.
The sinner sees Master Maudgalyāyana before his very eyes; Everyone weeps, their brows knit in grief.
It has been but a few months since my disciple died, Yet I, your compassionate father, truly do not know [of his fate].
Throughout our lives we have committed many sins, and only today, through great hardship, do we begin to repent.
Even if wives and concubines were to fill the mountains and rivers, who would be willing to die in our stead?
When shall we ever again part from the gates of the underworld? We report this to our children and grandchildren at home.
There is no need for a coffin and outer shell made of white jade;
Toiling in vain with gold to bury the grave mound brings no end to sorrow and lamentation. I hear no more the sounds of drums, music, and stringed songs.
If you wish to help the deceased escape suffering and hardship, Nothing surpasses cultivating merit to rescue their souls in the netherworld.
The Master, however, returned to transmit the teachings of the cessation of suffering.
He instructed that merit be cultivated to rescue those who have perished;
yet, with the exception of the Buddha alone, there is no means by which they can be saved.
I pray that the Upādhyāya will grasp the Nirvāṇa and never sink into the ordinary world, ferrying all sentient beings across;
may he diligently polish the wisdom-tongs to clear away the forest of afflictions, and may his majestic conduct pervade the world with universal compassion.
If the great vows of the Buddhas were to lead one out of the hells, it would be as if the compassionate father,
the Upādhyāya, were to descend universally;
Maudgalyāyana asked further about what occurs when proceeding forward.
At that time, as it approached midday, he arrived at the seat of the General of the Five Paths.
He asked his mother where she had gone to rest.
The nature of the General of the Five Paths was cruel; his golden armor shone brilliantly, and the light of his sword flashed and interlaced.
Surrounded by more than a million attendants on both sides, they all scrambled to catch the flying [deities],
their clamor like the roar of thunder shaking the earth; their eyes blazed with lightning,
some were seen cleaving open bellies or ripping out hearts, while others flayed the skin from their faces.
Although Maudgalyāyana was a sage, his soul was still startled and his eyes fell from their sockets as he wept for his compassionate mother;
though his supernatural powers were as swift as wind and clouds,
there is none who surpasses this Great General when it comes to the places of punishment on the dark path.
Spearmen crowd on both sides, blocking the great road; To the east and west stand more than ten thousand men.
Even if one raises their eyes to gaze toward the southwest, They see clearly the Five Way Gods guarding this path.
Having maintained this route for many kalpas, They settle the names of punishments for thousands of armies and myriads of multitudes.
From the beginning, each follows their own conditions and karma; This poor monk, like a compassionate mother, practices giving.
When souls drift along the paths of the underworld, If they head toward the three miserable realms, where will they suffer?
All say that the gates of the ghosts in the five destinies have opened; Beasts and evil humans wander about them in particular.
Those who love the Way enjoy the leisure of heaven morning and night; All sinners must pass through this place.
I pray that the General will examine us. The General joins his palms and says to the Ācārya:
"There is no need for you to weep and ruin your appearance; This road is usually crowded with walls and sand."
The Officer suddenly asked Qingti, "Do you know who this is? Taishan requires many named bureaus for investigation;
the Heavenly Court and the Earthly Registry each have their official documents and name-tokens.
A summons has descended to pass through this place; today, this disciple is an official by name.
"For a moment, let the Ācārya search and see; if the karmic fruit within can be met with by name, even seeking it out will not be difficult.
Then the General asked those around him, saying:
He asked whether he had seen Lady Qingti.
From the left side, a Du Guan official reported, saying,
"Three years ago, there was indeed a Lady Qingti."
He was summoned by a warrant from the Avīci Hell and was currently undergoing suffering there.
Upon hearing these words, Maudgalyāyana addressed [the Buddha], saying:
The general replied,
"Venerable Monk,
all criminals have their sentences determined by the King."
Then, as he first descended, Maudgalyāyana asked, "Mother, for what reason have you not seen the King's face?
She replied, "O Upādhyāya."
Among the two types of people in the world who are unable to see the King’s face,
the first type is one who, throughout their lifetime, cultivated the ten wholesome actions and the five precepts;
after death, their consciousness attains rebirth in the heavens.
As for the second type of person, they do not cultivate wholesome deeds while alive but extensively commit transgressions;
after their life ends, they enter hell and shall not even behold the face of the King.
"Only those who are half-evil and half-virtuous shall have their cases adjudicated upon seeing the King's face;
only then will they take rebirth and receive retribution according to their conditions.
Upon hearing these words, Maudgalyāyana immediately sought out his mother’s location among the various hells.
Maudgalyāyana sheds tears as he remembers his wandering; the karmic retribution of sentient beings is like the drifting of the wind.
His compassionate parents have reached a place of hardship and misery, their spirits already long since vanished.
Iron wheels constantly descend from the sky, and fierce fires burn beneath his feet at every moment.
The heart and viscera fall apart everywhere; the bones, sought out at once, seem scorched and withered like copper.
Ten thousand paths of bronze birds gaze toward the heart’s cavity; a thousand turns of iron hooks drench the crown of the head.
What was asked of the suffering beneath the sword-tree of old—how does it compare to having one's waist ground by a millstone and severed?
It cannot be described; it resembles congealed fat or shattered frost.
Vast and sprawling, it extends for several hundred *li*, towering down for one *yojana*.
Beneath it rest ten thousand iron spears, and a thousand layers of fire and smoke screen the four directions. If one asks what sin lies within this place:
Having finished saying, "This is the Hell of Killing Beings in Jambudvīpa," Maudgalyāyana proceeded further.
In a brief moment, he arrived at another hell and addressed the warden, saying:
"Is Lady Qingti in this hell?
I have come specifically to seek her out, for she is my mother.
The warden of the hell replied:
"Upādhyāya,
this prison consists entirely of men and there are no women at all.
If you go forward and ask about the Hell of the Mountain of Knives, you will certainly be able to see it."
Maudgalyāyana proceeded forward until he reached the hells.
To the left was the Mountain of Knives (Kṣuradhāra-parvata), and to the right was the Sword-Tree Forest (Asipattravana).
Within the hells, sharp blades pointed toward one another, and blood flowed in thin streams.
He saw the wardens of hell driving immeasurable sinners into this hell. Maudgalyāyana asked,
"What is the name of this hell?"
Rāṭha replied,
"This is the Hell of the Mountain of Knives and the Forest of Swords.
Maudgalyāyana asked:
"What kind of karmic offenses did the offenders in this prison commit to fall into this hell?
The warder replied,
"Regarding the lives of these offenders while they were still alive:"
Those who have encroached upon or damaged the permanent property of the monastery, who have wantonly used its water and fruit, or stolen its firewood—
today they shall hand over their bodies to the sword-trees,
where every limb and joint shall be severed and fall away.
Upon the mountain of blades, bleached bones lie scattered in chaos; In the forest of swords, there are thousands upon thousands of human heads.
If you wish not to climb that mountain of blades, Nothing surpasses filling the temple grounds with fertile soil and planting fruit trees within the monastery;
The seeds thus sown as offerings will multiply the permanent endowment.
"O you sinner, your offenses are unspeakable; for kalpas on end you have suffered through sins as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Though you followed the Buddha to nirvana, you still have not emerged from this hell. It stretches for hundreds of li from east to west;
the sinners run about in confusion, their shoulders jostling one another, as the karmic winds blow the flames forward to burn them."
The hell-wardens thrust their pitchforks from behind; their bodies and limbs are shattered like broken tiles, and their hands and feet are reduced to powder at that moment.
Boiling iron, leaping with light, is cast toward the mouth;
those who are struck pass through the left side as if it were a right-side hole. Copper arrows fly alongside, piercing the pupils of the eyes.
The sword-wheel descends straight through the air, slicing;
though it has not served anyone for a thousand years, the iron tongs gather and yet he returns to life. Hearing these words, Maudgalyāyana wept and sighed in lamentation.
He went forward and asked,
"Keeper of the prison, is there a Lady Qingti in this prison?"
The jailer addressed him, saying,
"Preceptor,
who is this relative of yours?"
Maudgalyāyana addressed him,
saying, "This is my compassionate mother.
The Lord of Hell replied:
"Upādhyāya,
in this prison there is no Lady Qingti;
previously, within the hells, they were all women."
They should have been able to see one another.
Upon hearing this, Maudgalyāyana proceeded further until he reached a certain hell that was one yojana in height and breadth.
Thick black smoke billowed forth, its stench reaching the heavens.
There he saw a horse-headed rākṣasa standing with an iron pitchfork grasped in his hand.
Maudgalyāyana asked,
"What is the name of this hell?
The rākṣasa replied:
"This is the Hell of the Copper Pillars and Iron Beds.
Maudgalyāyana asked,
"What karmic offenses did these sentient beings commit while alive that they have fallen into this hell?"
The warden replied,
"During her lifetime, this woman took men,
and this man took women, to engage in sexual intercourse."
Upon the bed of a mother-in-law;
upon the bed of a teacher or elder;
upon the bed of a master by a servant or slave.
When they fall into this hell,
their numbers in the east and west are beyond calculation;
men and women are equally divided.
The women lie upon iron beds with their bodies pierced by nails; The men embrace copper pillars until they are mangled and putrefied.
Iron drills with long, sharp blades cross and pierce them; Sharp fangs are like awls that bore through the intestines, Which are then filled with glowing iron balls;
When they cry out from thirst, they are drenched with molten iron.
Thorny burrs enter the belly like knives in the arms; Swords and halberds leap through the air amidst a chaos of falling stars.
Flesh and bone are hacked and shattered with a harsh crackling sound; Swords slice through liver and entrails, severing them inch by inch.
The hells and heavens stand as counterparts, beyond words to describe.
In heaven, joy resounds day and night;
in hell, no one seeks a way out. While one’s parents still live, perform meritorious deeds;
of the seven parts of the reward, one may obtain one. Even if the Eastern Sea were to turn into mulberry fields, [the merit would remain].
